Who Has the Power?, Canvas Calendar Events

BeCurrent · 5 topics · paste-ready

How to paste one of these

  1. Canvas Calendar, click the day, Edit, then More Options.
  2. Title the event exactly as given on the topic below.
  3. In the Rich Content Editor, click the </> icon to open the HTML editor. Never paste into the visual editor. Pasting rendered HTML there injects wrapper <div>s and inline font declarations that collapse the table.
  4. Press Copy the HTML below, then paste into that HTML editor.
  5. Switch back to the visual editor, delete the [INSERT ASSIGNMENT LINK] placeholder, and insert the real assignment from the right-hand course-links panel, Assignments, click the assignment. Do not hand-type that link; see Section 5 of CANVAS-BUILD-GUIDE.md for why.
  6. Save.

This file is generated

OVERVIEW, LEARNING TARGETS and SUCCESS CRITERIA are lifted verbatim from scripts/lib/unit-content/midterms.js. Edit a target there and rerun node scripts/build-canvas-events.js. Never edit a target in Canvas, and never in this file: both are copies, and nothing can tell you when a copy has gone stale.

The markdown twin is docs/canvas/midterms-calendar-events.md. It carries the same tables, built by the same function, so the two cannot disagree.

Topic 1

CE - WP1 - The Election Nobody Understands

What are voters actually choosing?

Event title
CE - WP1 - The Election Nobody Understands
Assignment to link
WP1 - What Midterms Change · 20 points
What it will look like in Canvas

OVERVIEW

Find out what is on the 2026 ballot, compare the House and Senate, and explain how Congress can change while the president stays in office.

LEARNING TARGETS
  1. I can explain what a midterm election changes and what it does not.
  2. I can distinguish House elections from Senate elections.
  3. I can explain one way a changed congressional majority could affect government decisions.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  1. I can identify congressional offices on the ballot and explain that the presidency is not being elected.
  2. I can sort at least four of five House/Senate facts correctly and correct my errors.
  3. I can use one verified fact to explain a possible governing consequence.

Topic 2

CE - WP2 - The Battle for Congress

How separate races become a majority

Event title
CE - WP2 - The Battle for Congress
Assignment to link
WP2 - The Battle for Congress · 20 points
What it will look like in Canvas

OVERVIEW

Follow individual seats to chamber control. Test how a small shift can change leaders, committees, and the agenda without guaranteeing a new law.

LEARNING TARGETS
  1. I can explain how individual elections determine chamber membership.
  2. I can explain how a majority affects leaders and committees.
  3. I can distinguish organizing a chamber from passing a law.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  1. I can identify the majority in a constructed 435-seat House scenario.
  2. I can identify two decisions a new majority could influence.
  3. I can explain one reason chamber control does not guarantee a policy change.

Topic 3

CE - WP3 - The Power to Stop a President

Checks, cooperation, and governing limits

Event title
CE - WP3 - The Power to Stop a President
Assignment to link
WP3 - Checks and Governing · 20 points
What it will look like in Canvas

OVERVIEW

Investigate laws, spending, oversight, and confirmations. Explain how Congress checks a president and why disagreement can create both accountability and delay.

LEARNING TARGETS
  1. I can explain ways Congress checks presidential power.
  2. I can explain why one election does not settle every governing decision.
  3. I can explain a benefit and a difficulty of divided government.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  1. I can accurately explain two congressional checks.
  2. I can explain why one chamber cannot ordinarily enact a law alone.
  3. I can support an accountability benefit and a governing difficulty with a specific example.

Topic 4

CE - WP4 - The Fight for Your Vote

Messages, evidence, and uncertainty

Event title
CE - WP4 - The Fight for Your Vote
Assignment to link
WP4 - Election Messages · 20 points
What it will look like in Canvas

OVERVIEW

Investigate campaign framing, check a real claim, and read a poll without treating it as an election result.

LEARNING TARGETS
  1. I can explain how a campaign message directs attention.
  2. I can check a claim against an independent source.
  3. I can distinguish a poll, a promise, and a verified result.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  1. I can identify a message’s claim, audience, and missing context.
  2. I can name a second source and explain what it supports, contradicts, or leaves unresolved.
  3. I can explain why a poll or promise does not establish what will happen.

Topic 5

CE - WP5 - Election Night: What Happens Next?

The 2026 results and their governing impact

Event title
CE - WP5 - Election Night: What Happens Next?
Assignment to link
WP5 - Results and Impact · 30 points
What it will look like in Canvas

OVERVIEW

Return after November 3 to record sourced 2026 results, identify unresolved races, and explain their possible governing effects. Separate established outcomes from predictions.

LEARNING TARGETS
  1. I can distinguish a projection, unofficial count, and certified result.
  2. I can connect the 2026 outcome to a governing consequence and a limit.
  3. I can support an explanation with two sources and a fair alternative interpretation.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  1. I can record House, Senate, and one Indiana result or unresolved race with sources, reporting stage, and a check date.
  2. I can explain two possible governing effects and one outcome that is not guaranteed.
  3. I can use two identified sources, address a competing interpretation, and state an uncertainty.
